title: Kestrel and the Weather
premise: Astrid Vasquez has spent fifteen years inspecting bridges and avoiding her own foundations: a marriage to dutiful, decent Marcus that she measures in millimeters of drift, and a past in the coastal town of Kestrel Point she fled after a fire that killed her brother. When her family's crumbling house goes up at auction, Astrid returns to bid on the wreckage of her childhood and collides with Jonah Reyes, the boy who loved her and whom she betrayed the night everything burned. As the auction deadline looms, Astrid must decide whether to keep the house as a monument to guilt or finally tell the truth about what happened—learning that memory, like steel, fails not from one load but from years of unexamined stress. She keeps the house, tells the truth, lets the marriage end honestly, and begins rebuilding—not the past, but herself.
about_author: Coral Sterling is a former structural engineer who spent a decade inspecting coastal infrastructure before turning to fiction full-time. Her work examines how people live inside structures—buildings, marriages, memories—that were never built to hold what they carry.

chapters.title: Load Ratings
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. On a routine bridge inspection, Astrid catalogs hairline fractures with clinical precision while her marriage to Marcus registers only as background noise—a missed anniversary, separate toothbrushes. The emotional beat is quiet numbness; she measures everything except herself.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. At home, Astrid moves through her own kitchen like a renter, noticing Marcus has repainted without asking her opinion. A colleague jokes that she lives like she's subletting her life. The beat is unease: invisibility feels safe, but something in her is starting to itch.

chapters.title: Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. A legal notice arrives: the Vasquez house in Kestrel Point, unclaimed since her mother's death, will be auctioned in six weeks. Astrid stares at the photograph of the sagging porch. The beat is vertigo—the past arriving by certified mail.

chapters.title: What Marcus Doesn't Ask
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus notices Astrid's distraction and chooses, as he always does, not to probe. He loves her carefully, the way you handle cracked glass. The beat is tender irony: his restraint, meant as kindness, is another wall between them.

chapters.title: Kestrel Point
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid drives to Kestrel Point for the first open house, passing the charred lot where the old boathouse stood. Townspeople recognize her and go quiet. The beat is dread braided with longing; the town remembers what she tried to bury.

chapters.title: Jonah
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. In the dusty hallway of the house, Astrid runs into Jonah Reyes—her brother Teo's best friend, the boy she loved, the witness to the fire. Fifteen years haven't softened his eyes. The beat is electric shock: the past has a face and it's looking right at her.

chapters.title: The Fire, Version One
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Flashback chapter: seventeen-year-old Astrid, Teo, and Jonah on the night of the boathouse fire—told as Astrid has always told it, an accident, a tragedy, no one's fault. The beat is the uncanny feeling of a story that doesn't quite fit its own shape.

chapters.title: Bidding War
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Back in the present, a developer outbids Astrid's opening offer, forcing her to commit money—and time—she doesn't have. Jonah, it turns out, works for the developer. The beat is rising stakes: to keep the house she must stay, and staying means facing him daily.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus visits Astrid mid-trip and finds her more alive than she's been in years—at a distance. He recognizes the drift between them the way she'd recognize corrosion: gradual, structural, possibly fatal. The beat is quiet heartbreak and dawning clarity.

chapters.title: Teo's Room
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Cleaning the house alone, Astrid finds Teo's untouched bedroom and a shoebox of letters—including ones Jonah wrote her after the fire that she never opened. The beat is grief cracking open; the sealed room becomes a sealed self.

chapters.title: Letters Unopened
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid reads Jonah's letters and learns he spent years trying to reach her, to share the weight of that night. She reads them in order and feels the story she's told herself begin to buckle under load. The beat is shame transforming into hunger for truth.

chapters.title: The Storm
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A storm traps Jonah and Astrid in the house overnight. He tells her what he saw that night—her leaving the boathouse before the fire, Teo going back in for something she'd left behind. The beat is confrontation; love and accusation arrive in the same voice.

chapters.title: Version Two
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Flashback retold truthfully: Astrid had stolen away to meet Jonah secretly, leaving her journal behind; Teo went back for it when the lantern tipped. The fire wasn't her crime, but her secrecy was its kindling. The beat is devastating self-recognition.

chapters.title: Confession
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid drives through the night and confesses the whole story to Marcus—not to be forgiven, but to stop hiding. Marcus listens without flinching. The beat is release and rupture: honesty costs her the marriage's comfortable fiction but returns her to ownership of her own life.

chapters.title: Separation Load
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus moves out—not in anger, but because he refuses to be loved by a tenant. His dignity and grief are quiet, final. The beat is mournful respect: two good people admitting the structure failed, not from betrayal but from never bearing weight together.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. At the auction, Astrid bids everything she has against the developer. Jonah, holding the developer's proxy, must choose—and steps aside, letting her win at her limit. The beat is climax-adjacent tension: the house, like her future, hangs on a single number.

chapters.title: Deed
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid signs for the house and stands in the empty rooms, owner at last of a place and a history. She opens every window. The beat is fragile triumph: possession without yet knowing what to build.

chapters.title: The Boathouse Lot
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah meets Astrid on the burned lot where Teo died. They speak plainly for the first time—grief shared instead of hoarded. He admits he stopped hating her years ago and hated himself instead. The beat is catharsis; forgiveness begins as a shared silence.

chapters.title: Blueprints
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid drafts plans to rebuild the boathouse as a public library wing in Teo's name, enlisting Jonah's construction firm. The town, wary, slowly warms. The beat is purpose: guilt converted into load-bearing structure.

chapters.title: Inspection
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. During demolition of the damaged east wall, workers find Teo's recovered journal, water-stained but legible—his own account of that night, full of love and no blame. Astrid reads it aloud to Jonah. The beat is grace arriving from rubble.

chapters.title: Kestrel and the Weather
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge at the library dedication. Rain threatens and holds off; the kestrels return to the bluff. Astrid speaks Teo's name in public for the first time. The beat is communal healing: the town, the brothers' memory, and Astrid all weathered, all standing.

chapters.title: Owner
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. One year later, Astrid inspects a bridge at dawn, then drives home to the house she keeps repaired, to Jonah, to a life she maintains deliberately. She signs her inspection report with a steady hand. The beat is earned peace: no longer a tenant of her days, but their author.
